content: The ammonium cation, represented by the chemical formula NH₄⁺, is a positively charged polyatomic ion. It is formed through the protonation of ammonia (NH₃). Ammonium and aminium are general terms used to describe positively charged or protonated substituted amines and quaternary ammonium cations (N⁺R₄), where one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by organic radical groups, symbolized as R. In the ammonium ion, the nitrogen atom, which carries a positive charge, forms four covalent bonds instead of the three typically seen in ammonia. This reaction is reversible. The ammonium ion can act as a very weak Brønsted-Lowry acid, meaning it can donate a proton to a stronger base by using one of its hydrogen atoms, thereby converting back to ammonia. This makes the ammonium ion the conjugate acid of the base ammonia. The extent to which ammonia forms ammonium ions in a solution depends on the pH of the solution. Additionally, ammonium compounds can form in the vapor phase. For instance, when ammonia vapor interacts with hydrogen chloride vapor, a white cloud of ammonium chloride forms, which eventually settles as a thin white solid layer on surfaces. Ammonium cations share similarities with alkali metal ions, such as Na⁺ or K⁺, and are found in salts like ammonium bicarbonate, ammonium chloride, and ammonium nitrate. Most simple ammonium salts are highly soluble in water. The ammonium ion behaves somewhat like an alkali metal ion. When attempting to receive an electron, the ammonium ion breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen. Ammonium ions can also dissolve in mercury to form an amalgam. Any hydrogen atom in the ammonium ion can be replaced with an alkyl or other organic radical group to form a substituted ammonium ion, also known as an aminium ion. Depending on the number of organic radical groups, these ions are classified as primary, secondary, tertiary, or quaternary ammonium cations. These substituted ammonium ions exist in equilibrium with their respective substituted amines, depending on the pH of the environment. However, quaternary ammonium cations are permanently charged. An example of a reaction forming an ammonium ion is the interaction between dimethylamine ((CH₃)₂NH) and an acid, resulting in the dimethylaminium cation ((CH₃)₂NH₂⁺). In biological systems, ammonium ions are toxic waste products of metabolism in animals. In humans, ammonium is converted into urea through the urea cycle, as urea requires less water for excretion. In aquatic animals, ammonium is excreted unchanged in the urine.
